title: What Makes a Trustworthy Church Leader
overview: Paul tells Timothy what kind of people should lead and serve in a local church, explains why it matters, and closes with six short lines about Jesus that many scholars think come from an early hymn.

parts.label: Overseers: what to look for (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: An overseer (older translations say 'bishop') led and cared for a local congregation, and most of the qualities asked for are plain good character: self-control, gentleness, honesty about money, welcoming guests, and the ability to teach. The marriage line reads literally 'a man of one wife,' and readers differ on whether it rules out having several wives, remarrying, or being unfaithful, which is why some translations say 'husband of one wife' and others 'faithful to his wife.'

parts.label: Home life and reputation (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: A leader's home was treated as a test case: someone who cannot care for a household well is unlikely to care well for a congregation (vv. 4-5). A new believer might grow proud and fall under the same judgment as the devil, and a bad name among people outside the church could bring disgrace and lead him into a trap (vv. 6-7).

parts.label: Deacons, the practical helpers (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: Deacons (from a Greek word meaning 'servant' or 'helper') seem to have handled practical work such as caring for the poor and looking after shared money, which may be why honesty and not chasing gain are stressed. They were to hold the faith sincerely and be examined before serving, though the text does not say how.

parts.label: Women, and deacons' homes (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: The Greek word in verse 11 can mean 'women' or 'wives,' so some read it as the wives of deacons and others as women who served as deacons, like Phoebe, whom Romans 16:1 describes with the same word used for a deacon. Verse 12 repeats the disputed 'man of one wife' phrase from verse 2 along with running a home well, and verse 13 says those who serve well gain good standing and confidence in their faith.

parts.label: God's household and the truth (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: Paul hopes to visit soon but writes in case he is delayed, picturing the church as God's household and as a pillar and base that holds the truth up for people to see. Protestant readers usually stress that the church holds up a truth resting on Christ, while Catholic and Orthodox readers also see here the church's role in guarding and teaching that truth.

parts.label: Six lines about Jesus (v. 16)
parts.note: These short balanced lines are widely thought to quote an early Christian hymn or creed, tracing Jesus from his life on earth, through being shown to be in the right (often linked to his resurrection), to his message spreading and his being taken up to heaven. Older manuscripts begin 'He who' while later ones read 'God,' so translations differ.

disagreement: Christians differ over how these roles relate to churches today, with Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches seeing them develop into the later ranks of bishops, priests and deacons while many Protestant churches treat overseers and elders as one local role, and they also differ over whether the wording of these lists limits leadership to men.
think: When you decide whether to trust someone with responsibility over others, how much weight do you give to how they live at home and how outsiders see them, compared with their skills?
